title: What should you ask first in a product launch case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a product launch case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first whether the decision to launch has already been made, and what the launch must achieve, because "should we launch?" and "how should we launch?" are different cases. The trap is jumping to product, price and promotion before you have chosen which customer the product is for.
body:
The first question to ask

Has the decision to launch been made, and what must the launch achieve?

If the client is still deciding, the case turns on whether the product will pay. If the decision is made, it turns on how to launch well: which customers, which channels, how fast. The goal matters too. A launch meant to defend share against a rival can accept thinner margins than one meant to add profit. Ask for a target (units, revenue, share) and a time frame.

How to build your structure

  • Who to target: segment size and growth, unmet needs, competitors in that segment.
  • What to offer: product, price, channels, message.
  • How to roll it out: capabilities needed; pilot, then scale.
  • Does it pay? Expected sales, costs, break-even, cannibalisation.

The full tree is in the product launch framework. For the "what to offer" branch, the 4Ps are a useful checklist, once the customer is chosen.

Give the launch a decision gate

A drinks company wants to launch a sugar-free drink. Before recommending a national campaign, check that it meets a clear customer need and that retailers will give it shelf space. Then build the numbers from the store up.

  • 500 stores × 40 bottles a week = 20,000 bottles a week
  • At $0.35 contribution a bottle: 20,000 × $0.35 = $7,000 a week
  • A $200k launch campaign pays back in $200k ÷ $7,000 ≈ 29 weeks, if sales hold

Now add cannibalisation. Suppose 40% of buyers would otherwise have bought the company's regular drink, which earns $0.45 a bottle. That is 8,000 bottles a week, or $3,600 of lost contribution. The real gain is $7,000 − $3,600 = $3,400 a week, and payback stretches to about 59 weeks. The new drink earns less per bottle than the one it replaces, so every switch costs the client $0.10.

So recommend a pilot in a representative set of stores, with a gate: national rollout only if repeat purchase, retailer reorders and net gain per store (after cannibalisation) hit agreed targets. A product that sells well is not a success if its sales mostly come from the client's own more profitable lines.

The trap most people fall into

Choosing the 4Ps before choosing the customer. Price, channel and message all depend on who you are selling to: a sugar-free drink for gym-goers is priced, placed and advertised differently from one for parents buying for children.

Weak: "I'd price it competitively, sell it in supermarkets and run a social media campaign."
Strong: "First, who is it for? If it's health-conscious adults who currently buy diet versions of rival brands, it wins share. If it's our own regular customers switching, it costs us 10 cents a bottle, so I'd want to know that split before spending on a campaign."

Two prompts to try

How should an insurer launch weather insurance for small farmers in Kenya?

Show the answer
  • Farmers' need: losses from drought and floods; what they can afford.
  • Product design: payouts triggered by rainfall data rather than claims inspections; price and cover.
  • Distribution: mobile money, co-operatives, seed sellers; bundling with loans.
  • Economics and risk: claims in a bad year; reinsurance, government support.

Where to start: distribution. Reaching small farmers cheaply decides whether it works.

The trap: designing a product farmers cannot pay for or reach.

Should a coffee chain launch a monthly subscription for unlimited filter coffee?

Show the answer
  • Target: regulars who already buy most days, or new customers drawn in by the offer.
  • Offer: price, what is included, limits per day.
  • Economics: revenue from subscribers against what they spent before; cost per extra cup; extra food sales.
  • Operations: queues at peak times; app and payment systems.

Where to start: cannibalisation. If most subscribers are regulars, the chain may simply be giving them a discount.

The trap: counting subscription revenue as new money.
